claims.text: Whole heart segmentation in congenital heart disease is challenged by extreme anatomical variability, limited labeled data, low cardiac MR signal-to-noise ratio and resolution, weak boundaries between structures, and stent artifacts.

The task labels LV, RV, LA including pulmonary veins, RA, AO, PA, SVC and IVC from a single-phase 3D cardiac MR scan and one click per structure; myocardium segmentation and time-series imaging are outside the stated focus.

The recurrent model uses a modified 3D U-Net to jointly predict the next segmentation and a stopping indicator, feeding the predicted segmentation into the next iteration. Users can override automatic stopping by selecting an earlier segmentation or requesting more iterations.

A teacher-forcing sequence likelihood loss decomposes into segmentation and stopping losses over decoupled time steps, eliminating backpropagation through time. Consecutive partial-segmentation training pairs are generated on the fly from complete ground truth.

Training targets prescribe constant-rate growth along vessel centerlines and outward chamber growth using concentric spheres intersected with ground truth. Input segmentations are corrupted with nonrigid deformations and foreground blobs while output targets remain unchanged.

The dataset contains 60 cardiac MR images with manual labels for eight structures: 20 HVSMR scans and 40 retrospectively retrieved clinical scans. All were acquired at Boston Children’s Hospital on a 1.5T Philips Achieva scanner.

Subjects ranged from younger than 1 to 55 years. Average image resolution was 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.85 mm; images were cropped around the heart and resized to 126 × 180 × 144. Severity categories described anatomical malformations, not clinical prognosis.

Experiments trained on 20 images and tested on 40, or trained on 48 images and tested on 12. Training used four-fold cross-validation, and the four resulting networks were ensembled for test predictions.
User interaction was simulated. Iter–U selected the best segmentation among the first 40 iterations, while Iter–U–All selected the iteration with the best mean accuracy across all eight structures.

For severe subjects with 20–HVSMR training, mean Dice scores across eight structures were 79.0 ± 17.2 for Iter–A, 85.3 ± 12.8 for Iter–U, 68.2 ± 27.8 for U–Net+S and 64.6 ± 31.9 for U–Net–All. Iter–A comparisons yielded p < 10^-11 versus U–Net+S and p < 10^-12 versus U–Net–All; both Iter–U comparisons yielded p < 10^-22.

For severe subjects with 48–HVSMR+ training, mean Dice scores were 85.1 ± 15.6 for Iter–A, 88.2 ± 14.0 for Iter–U, 82.0 ± 19.7 for U–Net+S and 84.9 ± 18.0 for U–Net–All. Iter–U significantly exceeded U–Net+S at p < 10^-2.

All seven methods performed well in mild/moderate subjects. Multiclass iterative models significantly improved over all three baselines with 20–HVSMR training, but no statistically significant overall improvements over the baselines were found with 48–HVSMR+ training.

Binary iterative inference required 0.65 ± 0.15 seconds per iteration on an NVIDIA TITAN X GPU, with mean structure segmentation times ranging from 2 to 18 seconds and approximately 1 minute for the whole heart.
Dice evaluation excluded optional vessel regions from both predicted and ground truth segmentations, comparing only required regions.

Failures included chamber growth through septal defects or valves and failure to grow through narrow or artifact-affected main pulmonary artery trunks. PA segmentation remained difficult generally, and some other structures remained difficult for particular pathologies.

Multiclass iterative models generally performed worse than binary models and gained less from simulated user stopping. A possible explanation is that a single multiclass iteration may not simultaneously provide the best segmentation of every structure; multiclass procedures were inherited from tuning for binary segmentation.
Actual-user accuracy and the hypothesis of faster, more intuitive interaction remain to be assessed in a user study; the reported experiments used simulated users.
The authors claim, to the best of their knowledge, the first whole heart segmentation that individually labels cardiac chambers and great vessels in cardiac MR for congenital heart disease patients.

The methodological contribution is an iterative segmentation framework with prescribed growth dynamics and a sequence loss using teacher forcing, enabling automatic stopping and optional selection among evolving segmentation candidates.
